title: Appetite grows into a life unless the Guru interrupts it
subtitle: Raag Maajh · Ang 137
summary: This shabad traces craving from infancy to death with unsentimental precision — milk, family, play, food, sexual desire, wealth, anger, decline, cremation. The pattern is not harmless just because it is familiar; without the Guru, the soul is left asking where to go as the world drowns.
whyItMatters: Craving often feels like personality because it has been rehearsed for so long. This shabad gives appetite a biography, showing how small loves harden into a whole direction unless the Guru teaches the soul another way to live.
takeaway: Name appetite early, before it names the whole life.

lines.translation: First, the baby loves mother's milk;
second, he learns of his mother and father;
third, his brothers, sisters-in-law and sisters;
fourth, the love of play awakens.
Fifth, he runs after food and drink;
sixth, in his sexual desire, he does not respect social customs.
Seventh, he gathers wealth and dwells in his house;
eighth, he becomes angry, and his body is consumed.
Ninth, he turns grey, and his breathing becomes labored;
tenth, he is cremated, and turns to ashes.
His companions send him off, crying out and lamenting.
The swan of the soul takes flight, and asks which way to go.
He came and he went, and now, even his name has died.
After he left, food was offered on leaves, and the birds were called to come and eat.
O Nanak, the self-willed manmukhs love the darkness.
Without the Guru, the world is drowning. ||2||

structure: The shabad follows desire through the ordinary stages of life, refusing to romanticize how attachment grows.
It shows appetite maturing into possession, anger, bodily decline, death, and the soul’s disoriented departure.
It closes with the sharp diagnosis: without the Guru, the world’s familiar loves still leave it drowning.

evidence.coreClaim: The shabad maps the lifelong growth of appetite and attachment, ending with the soul lost without the Guru.
evidence.turn: The sequence turns ordinary development into moral revelation — what begins as natural appetite can become a drowning life when no Guru interrupts it.
evidence.practicalImplication: Do not excuse a craving because it has a long history. Bring it under the Guru’s teaching while there is still time to redirect the life.
